# Cap load and quadratic reserve on the logarithmic boundary defect

This is a consequence of the actual common physical separator at the selected minima. It retains a positive next-order term that disappears from the ordinary unscaled stress. It does not assert defect exclusion or a sharp depth bound.

## 1. Abstract hypotheses supplied by the selected sequence

On a fixed compact normal/physical space let eta_j be the sampled boundary measures with their continuous outer normals recorded. Their masses are uniformly bounded and eta_j converges weakly to eta. Let positive finite-PL concave L_j converge uniformly on the relevant common compact set to L>=0. Put

    ell_j=-log L_j,  ell=-log L,  Z={L=0}.

Assume eta(Z)=0 and integral ell_{j,+} d eta_j<=C. The contact-gradient trace bound, uniform L_max and the zero-face codimension theorem supply these hypotheses. In particular ell_+ is integrable against eta by truncation and weak convergence.

Let 0<=W_j<=1 be the SAME allocated cap loads, beta_j->beta, and lambda_j>0 tend to zero. Suppose

    Xi_j=W_j-beta_j+lambda_j ell_j+R_j,
    |R_j|<=C lambda_j,                                      (1)

and the actual common separator satisfies

    integral Xi_j psi(u) Phi(w) d eta_j<=0                   (2)

for every continuous psi>=0 and every globally finite convex Phi. Suppose W_j eta_j converges weakly to W eta, retaining the actual cap-selector limit. After passing to a subsequence all finite positive measures used below have weak limits.

In the selected logarithmic-scale application lambda_j=Delta_j/((d+1)M_j)=tau_j/(d+1). The bounded energy, covariance and constant corrections give (1) pointwise; this is stronger than their vanishing surface L1 norm. Equation (2) is supplied by the fully audited common normal-dependent cone. The tests may depend on j, because each separator works for every such test at that fixed j.

## 2. Two boundary defects and a new positive reserve

Define

    b_j=ell_{j,+} eta_j,    a_j=W_j ell_{j,+} eta_j.

Their uniformly bounded masses and 0<=a_j<=b_j give subsequential limits. Away from Z, uniform convergence of logarithms and of the bounded normal/selector measures identifies those limits. Consequently they have the form

    b_j -> ell_+ eta+b,
    a_j -> W ell_+ eta+a,
    0<=a<=b,   support(a),support(b) subset Z.             (3)

These assertions follow first on compact sets where L is bounded away from zero, and then by exhaustion. Since eta(Z)=0, the residual measures are nonnegative restrictions to Z. The measure a is the actual log-weighted cap-load defect; it is not an independently assigned selector on the limiting zero faces.

There is also a uniformly bounded positive measure

    q_j=lambda_j ell_{j,+}^2 eta_j.                        (4)

Indeed test (2) with psi=1 and Phi=(ell_j-1)_+. This is convex on a neighborhood of the current body, and has a globally finite convex extension agreeing there, as justified in Section 3. On its support ell_j>1. Equations (1)--(2) give

    lambda_j integral ell_j(ell_j-1)_+ d eta_j
       <=(1+C lambda_j) integral ell_{j,+} d eta_j.

Since s^2<=s(s-1)_++s for s>=0, (4) has bounded mass. Its weak limit q is nonnegative and supported on Z: on a compact set where L>0, ell_j is bounded and lambda_j->0. The reserve q may be zero; no positive lower bound is assumed.

## 3. A perspective logarithm supplies all positive convex tests

For T real and a,b>0 put

    F_T(a,b)=max{0, a log(a/b)-T a}.

The relative-entropy perspective a log(a/b) is jointly convex. Subtracting T a and taking the maximum with zero preserves convexity. F_T is nondecreasing in a: on its positive branch the derivative is log(a/b)-T+1>1, and on its zero branch it is constant. It is nonincreasing in b.

For any globally finite convex f that is strictly positive on a neighborhood of the common body range, the composition

    Phi_{j,T}(w)=F_T(f(w),L_j(w))
               =f(w)[ell_j(w)+log f(w)-T]_+               (5)

is convex wherever L_j>0. To verify composition directly, use convexity of f, concavity of L_j, the two stated monotonicities, and joint convexity of F_T in that order. Every current compact body lies in an open convex neighborhood where L_j>0 and f>0. On a slightly larger compact neighborhood the subgradients of (5) are bounded. The supremum of its supporting affine functions based on the smaller neighborhood is therefore a globally finite convex extension equal to (5) at every current boundary point. This makes (5) an actual allowed test; no uniform bound on its j-dependent slopes is claimed or needed.

Fix T>sup log f on the common compact range and write c(w)=T-log f(w)>0. Then

    Phi_{j,T}=f(ell_j-c)_+
             =f ell_{j,+}-f min{ell_{j,+},c}.              (6)

For fixed T the last minimum is a bounded continuous function of (L_j,w), extending continuously to L_j=0 by the value c(w). Uniform convergence of L_j therefore permits it as a weak-limit test of both eta_j and W_j eta_j.

## 4. The exact limiting inequality

The R_j term in (2), tested with psi Phi_{j,T}, tends to zero, because its absolute value is bounded by a constant times lambda_j integral ell_{j,+}. Equations (3) and (6) give

    lim integral psi(W_j-beta_j)Phi_{j,T} d eta_j
      =integral psi(W-beta) f(ell-c)_+ d eta
          +integral psi f d(a-beta b).                    (7)

On the positive branch of (5), ell_j>c>0. Furthermore

    |lambda_j ell_j Phi_{j,T}-f lambda_j ell_{j,+}^2|
       <=lambda_j f c ell_{j,+}.

Its integral tends to zero. Thus the logarithmic term in (2) tends to integral psi f dq. Combining this with (7), then letting T->infinity, proves

    integral psi(u) f(w) d(a+q)
        <=beta integral psi(u) f(w) db.                    (8)

Dominated convergence in the last step uses integrability of ell_+ against eta; the ordinary truncated logarithmic tail vanishes. Replacing a nonnegative convex f by f+delta and sending delta down to zero extends (8) to every nonnegative globally finite convex f. All functions remain bounded on the common compact range.

In particular

    a(total)+q(total)<=beta b(total).                      (9)

The same inequality holds after localization by any nonnegative continuous function of the recorded normal. Equation (8) is a normal-localized positive-convex-order constraint. It contains a mass deficit, so it must not be replaced by an equality of affine moments or by an ordinary probability martingale.

## 5. Scope and dependence

The boundary defect b is coupled to the inverse-volume defect by the separate Gauss--Green theorem. Equation (8) adds actual cap-selector information and a positive quadratic logarithmic reserve. It permits b>0 and does not identify the cap load at a coincident limiting plane with its closed-halfspace indicator. Nor does it identify surface and volume allocations without the separately proved vector identity.

The new conclusion is stronger than discarding the O(lambda_j) corrections against uniformly bounded tests: the convex tests (5) deliberately grow in the logarithmic boundary layer. Every use of that growth is controlled by the exact positive term in (1) and by the uniform trace bound. No exchange of a fixed-limit body derivative with a prelimit derivative is used.
